Umami is a distinct fifth basic taste, scientifically identified by Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda in 1908 and characterized as a savory, brothy, or meaty flavor. It is detected by specific taste receptors which respond to glutamates - commonly added as MSG - and ribonucleotides like IMP and GMP, which are naturally present in foods like meat, fish, mushrooms, and fermented products. The discovery of the synergistic effect between glutamates and nucleotides deepened the understanding of umami's intensity in foods such as dashi, cheese, and soy sauce. Following its identification, Ikeda co-founded Ajinomoto to commercialize MSG, spreading umami seasoning worldwide, and subsequent research confirmed dedicated umami receptors on the tongue and in the stomach.
